newsitem.title: FRANCE: French stocks seen falling further on poll results.
newsitem.headline: French stocks seen falling further on poll results.

text.p: The French stockmarket, which lost six percent last week, is expected to fall further, traders and analysts said after early projections pointed to a Socialist-led win in Sunday's parliamentary election runoff vote.
Equities strategist Gary Dugan at J.P. Morgan said he expected the Paris bourse's CAC-40 index to fall next week but not more than three percent.

"This is better than the worst outcome, which would have been a heavy reliance on the Communists for an absolute majority," Dugan said on projections giving the Socialists and their allies other than the Communists an outright majority.
"It seems the Socialists are going to be able to form a government without the Communists. This is relatively good news," said Marie Owens-Thomsen, economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
She said the CAC-40 index, which finished down 6.48 percent last week at 2,583.94 points, could fall to 2,500. "I would be surprised to see it go much lower," she said.
Paribas economist Dominique Barbet said, "I think the reaction will not be positive, but if the Socialists get an outright majority, the markets' fall should be relatively limited."

Barbet said he expected the stockmarket to show the biggest reaction again, as it did after the left won the first-round last Sunday, because of the greater presence of foreign investors who hold about 40 percent of the Paris stockmarket.

Elisabetta Castelli, head of international equities CDC Bourse, said that although the election has lifted some of the uncertainty weighing on the bourse, investors will remain anxious until the new government outlines its programme.
"We will be waiting on the lips of the politicians. There will be considerable volatility as announcements come through on policy decisions," she said.
"Until we get an absolutely clear indication on France Telecom, I see privatisation stocks and restructuring stories continuing to underperform," Dugan said.
He said the decision on France Telecom's partial privatisation -- scheduled by the outgoing government to begin in the coming week -- would be key "to judge how left-wing this government will be".
Carmaker Renault, whose restructuring plans may be put in doubt, is also likely to weaken further, he said.
"We don't know whether France Telecom and Thomson-CSF will be privatised," Castelli said.

Michelle Jardin, equities strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities, said the bourse would probably lose another two percent or so in the week, "but I think over the next few months, it will be all right".

"The sectors that perform best after victories by the left are consumer goods, retailers and exporters. The most negatively affected are financials and industrials as we saw in the past week. We can expect this to continue next week," she said.
"We could lose 50 to 100 points tomorrow," said Olivier Blitz, senior trader at IFF Bourse, whose recent market forecasts have been among the more pessimistic and accurate.
The bourse's performance will be strongly influenced by the makeup of the new government, he said.

Communist Party leader Robert Hue's remarks on Sunday that he would ask for ministries based on the party's strong showing estimated at 35 or 36 seats out of a total of 577 would be taken badly, particularly by foreign investors, he said.
He said the bourse could open at around 2,530 points, which represents a strong technical support level. "If we break through that, it could fall to 2,450," he said.

A survey of 10 brokerage firms conducted last week showed they expected the CAC index to fall to between 2,380 and 2,525 if the left won the parliamentary election and to rise to between 2,600 and 2,750 if the centre-right coalition was returned to power.
-- Christine Tierney, Paris Newsroom, +33 1 4221 5452
